title: A Look at Dobbers Quest for the Key
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zVMIZRDSvCc

Daniel (@dungeondive) goes looking for a hidden gem on a clearance page and comes back with Darryl T. Jones's *Dobbers Quest for the Key* — an adventure deck-builder bought mostly because the box art looked unlike everything else on the shelf.

The pitch: think Clank!, but instead of descending a dungeon you build a deck and push a meeple across a land toward a central space holding the key. Cards feed three currencies — travel points, challenge points, and universal points that serve either. Items, weapons and armour do nothing in hand; they must be equipped, one per slot, and carry navigation, protection, combat or travel icons that ease specific challenges. Purple cards cull your deck, and four card colours reward building toward synergy.

The mechanism Daniel finds genuinely clever is that players build the board for each other. Location and creature cards are purchased and placed into empty spaces, then unwanted equipment gets sandwiched between them — whoever beats the challenge stack claims the gear. He compares it to the old *Venture Forth* and to *Dungeoneer*.

The honest verdict: the solo mode is thin, and he'd reach for *Hand of Fate: Ordeals* instead. This is a competitive game, and not a hidden gem — just a decent, cheap, quick one, carried by art he wants to see more of.

----

Daniel bought this almost entirely on the strength of its art — and says the solo mode isn't where it shines. When has a game's look alone justified the purchase for you?
